consensus_summary: Primary Christian consensus: clean/unclean symbolizes moral-spiritual purity versus sin-defilement/unfitness for God's presence; cleanse/cleansing symbolizes forgiveness, purification and sanctification accomplished through Christ (OT rites as types). Alternatives (often scholarly) include non-moral ritual/cultic status, Israelite boundary-markers, symbolic order/wholeness, death-life, or hygiene.
book_summary: Cleansing removes the defilement that bars proper contact, approach or use; clean means free of that defilement and fit for its permitted place. Uncleanness may be physical, ceremonial or moral and does not always equal guilt (e.g., childbirth, marital relations, corpse contact). Cleansing merely restores fitness; sanctification then places the cleansed vessel under holy claim and appointed use.
consensus_core_identification: Moral/spiritual purity versus sinful defilement; cleansing = divine forgiveness + sanctification (OT as type).
book_core_identification: Any defilement (physical/ceremonial/moral) that bars proper contact/approach/use; cleansing restores fitness (not always guilt); distinct from sanctification.
boundary_disagreement: Book treats non-moral ritual cases (childbirth, sex, corpse) as genuine uncleanness without guilt and sharply separates cleansing (removal of barrier) from sanctification (holy appointment); consensus primary often collapses uncleanness to sin and cleansing to forgiveness/sanctification, relegating non-moral cases to alternatives or typology.
material_contradiction: None; moral uses and Christ's blood cleansing remain fully included.
rationale: Both share the basic purity/fitness-for-approach category. The book keeps that referent but materially broadens and re-precisifies its extension: multi-type uncleanness (explicitly not always guilt) becomes definitional rather than secondary, and cleansing is analytically distinguished from sanctification against the common conflation. This is boundary refinement, not replacement of the central idea of fitness for holy contact.
strongest_objection: Dominant confessional use equates the terms to moral purity and Christ's sanctifying work; the book's multi-category functional emphasis (and cleansing/sanctification split) can appear to dilute or de-emphasize that primary spiritual reading.
